rationale: Per-drug signal strength varies a lot (strong for targeted oncology drugs, near-noise for many non-oncology ones), so one shared alpha=5000 over-shrinks some drugs and under-shrinks others. I'm swapping in efficient leave-one-out (GCV) RidgeCV that picks a separate alpha for each drug on the training fold only. It uses the same features and is still one fast closed-form multi-output fit. I haven't run this candidate, so its Dev score is unknown.

A lot of PRISM sensitivity follows lineage. In the current model that signal is spread thinly over 5,000 genes that are all shrunk heavily at alpha=5000. This change adds one-hot OncotreeLineage columns scaled by a weight w, so the lineage effect is penalised much less than single genes. w is chosen by grouped inner CV on the training fold only, and w=0 is one of the options, so the model can fall back to the current solution. I haven't run this candidate, so its Dev score is unknown.

Many PRISM drugs share a few response axes, such as general cytotoxic or proliferation sensitivity and lineage programs. For weak drugs, each drug's own ridge prediction is mostly noise, so I'm turning the ridge into a reduced-rank ridge. Predictions are projected onto the top-k right singular vectors of the fitted drug×line response, which pools signal across similar drugs. k is chosen by grouped inner CV on the training fold only, and full rank is one of the options, so the model can fall back to the current solution. I haven't run this, so its Dev score is unknown.

The current ridge treats each drug's own target genes like the other 5,000 variable genes, so it shrinks them heavily (or drops them if their variance is low). Yet target expression is the most direct biological sensitivity marker for targeted drugs such as EGFR, BRAF or BCL2 inhibitors. This change adds each drug's target-gene expression (from `ctx["drugs"].target`) through a per-drug kernel ridge, `K = XXᵀ + w·T_dT_dᵀ`, so target genes are penalised `w` times less than other genes. One shared `w` is chosen by grouped inner CV on the training fold only, and `w=0` is one of the options, which reproduces the current model exactly. I haven't run this, so its Dev score is unknown.

The ridge model is purely linear, but drug sensitivity often follows non-additive similarity between cell lines, for example lines that share a lineage or transcriptional state responding alike. This change blends the linear kernel with a centered Gaussian (RBF) kernel built on the same 5,000 standardized genes: K = (1−v)·K_lin + v·s·K_rbf. The scale s matches the RBF kernel's trace to the linear kernel's, so the overall prior variance (and so the effective alpha) stays about the same. The blend weight v and the target-gene weight w are chosen together by grouped inner CV on the training fold only. Setting v=0 reproduces the current model exactly. I haven't run this candidate, so its Dev score is unknown.

For many drugs the target genes themselves are weak markers or barely vary across cell lines, but the targets' STRING interaction partners (same complex or pathway) often carry the sensitivity signal. This change adds each drug's top-30 STRING first-degree neighbours of its targets as a third per-drug kernel block, scaled by its own weight `wn` and normalised by neighbourhood size. `wn` is chosen jointly with (v, w) by grouped inner CV on the training fold, and `wn=0` reproduces the current model exactly.

Many lines were never measured on some drugs. Right now those gaps are filled with the drug's mean AUC and fitted as if they were real values, which adds label noise and pulls each drug's fit toward flat. This change fits the kernel ridge for each drug only on the lines where that drug was actually measured. Complete drugs are still solved together in one batch. Missing values are no longer imputed, either inside the training-fold CV that picks (v, w) or in the final fit. I haven't run this candidate, so its Dev score is unknown.

This adds pathway-level expression scores as a third kernel block, penalised less than single genes. Each score is the mean z-scored expression of a Hallmark or Reactome gene set, computed with training-fold statistics, and each collection is weighted equally. Coordinated programs such as EMT, proliferation, interferon, KRAS or MYC signalling and oxidative phosphorylation should be more stable sensitivity markers than individual noisy genes, and they can use genes outside the top-5,000 by variance. The weight u is chosen jointly with (v, w) by grouped inner CV on the training fold, and u=0 reproduces the current model exactly. I haven't run this candidate, so its Dev score is unknown.

Right now each of the 5,000 genes is z-scored, so low-expressed, noisy genes count as much as the high-variance lineage and state markers that usually drive PRISM sensitivity. This change scales genes by sd^-p (p=1 is the current z-scoring, p=0.5 is partial, p=0 is raw centred log-TPM) and rescales the result so total feature variance stays the same, which keeps the effective alpha unchanged. The RBF bandwidth is recomputed for each p. p is chosen jointly with (v, w) by grouped inner CV on the training fold only, and ties go to p=1, so the current model can always be recovered. I haven't run this candidate, so its Dev score is unknown.

Keep the current model but let grouped inner CV on the training fold also choose the ridge penalty, jointly with (v, w), from alpha ∈ {2000, 5000, 12500}. The fixed alpha = 5000 was tuned when the model was plain linear ridge. Adding the RBF blend, the target-gene block and fitting only on measured lines all change how much shrinkage is best. Round 1 failed because a separate alpha for each drug was too noisy, so here one shared alpha is used for all drugs. Ties go to alpha = 5000, which keeps the current model available.

I'm adding sharing across drugs with the same mechanism of action (MOA). Drugs that share an MOA label in `ctx["drugs"].moa` (for example "EGFR inhibitor", "tubulin polymerization inhibitor" or "HDAC inhibitor") act on the same biology, so for weak drugs, averaging their predicted sensitivity profiles should cancel noise better than pooling across all drugs. Round 3 pooled across all drugs at once with a low-rank projection, and that failed. Each drug's prediction gets b × the mean of its MOA partners' standardized predictions, rescaled to the drug's own AUC SD. b is chosen jointly with (alpha, v, w) by grouped inner CV on the training fold only, and b=0 reproduces the current model exactly. I haven't run this candidate, so its Dev score is unknown.

MOA sharing helped (round 11), but MOA labels are sparse and noisy: many drugs have unique labels, and drugs with different labels can still hit the same biology. This change adds a second sharing step. Each drug's prediction is also boosted by c × the weighted mean standardized prediction of its 10 most positively correlated drugs, with correlations computed from the training-fold AUC profiles (inside inner CV, only from the inner-train lines). c is chosen jointly with (alpha, v, w, b) by grouped inner CV on the training fold, and c=0 reproduces the current model exactly. I haven't run this candidate, so its Dev score is unknown.

PRISM AUCs have a few extreme responder or outlier lines per drug, and with squared loss those points dominate each drug's kernel-ridge fit, its mean/sd and the drug–drug correlations used for sharing. This change lets grouped inner CV choose whether to winsorize each drug's training AUCs at median ± 2.5·(1.4826·MAD) before fitting. Clipping uses only the training lines, and inner-CV scores are still computed against the raw AUCs. Not clipping (k=None) is one of the options and wins ties, so the current model can always be recovered. I haven't run this candidate, so its Dev score is unknown. Grouped inner CV now fits every setting once per clipping option, so the CV should take about twice as long. I haven't measured this against the ~25-minute limit.

Make the kernel's notion of cell-line similarity multi-task supervised. Right now all 5,000 variable genes count equally in both the linear and RBF kernels, so genes that vary for reasons unrelated to response (immune infiltration, sex genes, stress) dilute the signal. This change scales each gene's kernel contribution by s_g^q, where s_g is the gene's mean squared correlation with all 200 drugs' AUCs. That pools evidence across drugs, so it stays stable even though per-drug signal is weak. s_g is computed only on the (inner-)training lines and winsorized labels. The total trace is kept fixed so alpha means the same thing, and q ∈ {0, 1} is chosen jointly by grouped inner CV. q=0 wins ties and reproduces the current model exactly.

Add a third post-hoc sharing step that pools predictions across drugs with overlapping target genes. Each drug gets e × the Jaccard-weighted mean standardized prediction of drugs whose `ctx["drugs"].target` sets overlap its own. This catches drugs with the same biology whose MOA wording differs (e.g. "EGFR inhibitor" vs "tyrosine kinase inhibitor"), and unlike label correlations it doesn't depend on noisy, weak per-drug signal. e is chosen jointly with (k, alpha, v, w, b, c) by grouped inner CV on the training fold, and e=0 wins ties, which reproduces the current model exactly. I haven't run this candidate, so its Dev score is unknown.

PRISM AUCs share a strong cell-line-level "general sensitivity" factor g (linked to growth rate and overall drug susceptibility). Because g is averaged over 200 drugs it is much less noisy than any single drug, but the shared alpha is tuned for weak per-drug signals and so over-shrinks it. This change adds a correction, β_j·(ridge_{r·α}(g) − ridge_α(g)), which refits each drug's projection onto g with a smaller penalty r·α. The ratio r is chosen jointly by grouped inner CV on the training fold, and r=1 reproduces the current model exactly and wins ties.

The RBF kernel's bandwidth is set to the median squared distance across 5,000 dimensions. Because pairwise distances concentrate in high dimensions, exp(−d²/med) varies almost linearly with d². The current RBF block is therefore close to a rescaled linear kernel, which would explain why it only adds a little. This change lets grouped inner CV also choose a 4× narrower bandwidth (γ = 4/med). That gives a truly local similarity, so close transcriptional neighbours (lineage or subtype clusters) share sensitivity non-additively. The scale is still trace-matched, and the median bandwidth wins ties, so the current model can always be recovered. Inner CV now fits 5 kernel settings per alpha instead of 3, so it should take about 1.7× as long. I haven't measured this against the ~25-minute limit, and I haven't run the candidate, so its Dev score is unknown.

The kernel ridge spreads each drug's weight over 5,000 genes, so it dilutes sparse single-gene markers, such as SLFN11 for DNA-damaging agents or the gene in a drug's own MOA pathway, especially markers outside the top-5,000 by variance. This change adds a second, sparse per-drug model and blends it in by a weight λ before the MOA/correlation sharing step. For each drug, the sparse model picks the 50 genes (out of the 10,000 most variable) most correlated with that drug's measured training AUCs, then fits a ridge on just those genes. λ is chosen jointly with the other settings by grouped inner CV on the training fold, and λ=0 wins ties, so the current model is still available. I haven't run this candidate, so its Dev score and runtime against the ~25-minute limit are unknown.

The sparse per-drug biomarker model gave the largest single gain so far, but it always uses 50 genes per drug, and that number was never tuned. Some drugs probably have a few dominant markers (SLFN11 for DNA damage, the drug's target or its lineage driver) where 50 genes adds noise. Other drugs have broad transcriptional programs, where a larger set should be more stable. This change lets grouped inner CV on the training fold choose the number of genes, m ∈ {20, 50, 150}, jointly with the other settings. m=50 wins ties, so the current model can always be recovered. All three sizes come from one shared correlation ranking, so the extra cost is small. I haven't run this candidate, so its Dev score and its runtime against the ~25-minute limit are unknown.

With about 380 lines and weak per-drug signal, picking each drug's top-50 genes by correlation is unstable, so the single sparse ridge is high-variance. This change adds a bagged sparse model: 8 runs on 80% row subsamples (fixed seeds), each repeating the per-drug top-50 selection and ridge fit, then averaged. The goal is to keep stable markers and average out the spurious ones. Grouped inner CV on the training fold picks bagged or single (single wins ties) jointly with the existing settings. Picking single reproduces the current model. I haven't run this candidate, so its Dev score and runtime are unknown.
